::: notes
0–2. Animated, about 8 seconds. This is a room of physicists: the physics track is one sourced fact, and they know the rest better than we do. The first Monte Carlo calculations ran on ENIAC in April–May 1948 (Metropolis and Ulam published the method in *JASA* 44, 1949). History had its moment too. Le Roy Ladurie wrote the programmer line in “L’historien et l’ordinateur”, *Le Nouvel Observateur*, 8 May 1968, reprinted in *Le territoire de l’historien* (1973), pp. 11–14; the English is a translation, and wordings vary. Cliometrics, economic history done with statistics and computers, peaked with Fogel and Engerman’s *Time on the Cross* (1974). Gutman’s *Slavery and the Numbers Game* (1975) and *Reckoning with Slavery* (David, Gutman, Sutch, Temin, Wright and Stampp, 1976) contested its numbers and its inferences. Stone’s essay (*Past & Present* 85, 1979) framed narrative’s revival as a reaction against social-science history. Blevins (2016) asked why digital history still talks about potential. Your framing: why physics and not history? The skills barrier, the cost in time, and being tied to particular software. [Jim: add or swap one example from your own experience.]
:::

## What arrives at *Historical Methods* now {#jim-slop}

[I co-edit *Historical Methods*, a journal for quantitative and digital history. The cost of writing has collapsed, and it shows in what arrives.]{.lede}

::: {.defs}
::: {.def}
[Slop]{.def-term}
A fluent, generated paper with no research behind it.
:::

::: {.def}
[Semi-slop]{.def-term}
A real question or real data, with analysis and prose that nobody has checked.
:::
:::

```{=html}
    <div class="mrow rise" data-at="1900"><b>Prose</b><span><s data-at="2700" class="strike-on">months of drafting</s> minutes for a fluent draft</span></div>

  </div>

    <div class="mrow rise" data-at="4900"><b>Review</b><span>a referee still reads every page and checks every source</span></div>
    <div class="mfoot flat rise" data-at="5500">→ unchanged</div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="motion-caption rise" data-at="6400">There is no market for a ton more written history. The speed is only worth having if it buys better work.</p>
<p class="mq rise" data-at="7400">What does better look like? Two examples, then the evidence from one large project.</p>
```

::: notes
2–4. Animated, about 7 seconds. This is the turn of the talk. Production has collapsed in cost: code (Jessica went from never using a command line to interactive maps in under a month) and prose (a fluent draft takes minutes). Demand has not moved: readers, referees and journal pages are the same as before. More history, at this point, mostly costs other people time. So the question for the rest of the hour is what the speed should be spent on. [Jim: the "weeks" and "months" are illustrative; say them in your own terms.]
:::
